title: ISRO Test-Fires GSLV Cryogenic Engine for 200 Seconds Ahead of NVS-04 Launch
excerpt: The CE-7.5 engine cleared its flight acceptance hot test at the ISRO Propulsion Complex in Mahendragiri on November 5, and will now be fitted into the cryogenic stage of the GSLV-F19 mission that will carry the NVS-04 navigation satellite.
body:
• ISRO completed a 200-second flight acceptance hot test of the CE-7.5 cryogenic engine on November 5 at its propulsion complex in Mahendragiri, Tamil Nadu, with the engine's performance reported as nominal throughout.
  • The engine will be inducted into the cryogenic upper stage of GSLV-F19, the mission that will launch NVS-04, the fourth satellite in India's second-generation NavIC series.
  • Both the main engine and the gas generator ignited as expected, and steady-state performance matched predictions, according to ISRO's update shared on November 10.
  • NVS-04 follows the October 30 launch of NVS-03; with NVS-05, it completes the planned five-satellite NVS series. ISRO has not announced a GSLV-F19 launch date.

The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) has successfully completed the flight acceptance hot test of the CE-7.5 cryogenic engine that will power the upper stage of the GSLV-F19 mission, the flight that will carry the NVS-04 navigation satellite into orbit. The engine fired for 200 seconds at the ISRO Propulsion Complex (IPRC) in Mahendragiri, Tamil Nadu, on November 5, and its performance remained nominal throughout the test, according to an ISRO update shared on November 10.

What the test showed

A flight acceptance test is the final ground check an engine must pass before it is cleared to fly. ISRO said both the main engine and the gas generator ignited as expected during the firing, and that the engine's performance in steady-state operation was normal and consistent with predictions. With the test complete, the engine will now be inducted into the cryogenic stage of the GSLV-F19 launch vehicle.

The engine: India's own cryogenic upper stage

The CE-7.5 is an indigenously developed cryogenic engine that powers the third, upper stage of the GSLV Mk-II. It burns liquid hydrogen with liquid oxygen — propellants stored at extremely low temperatures — on a fuel-rich staged-combustion cycle, and produces a nominal thrust of about 73.5 kilonewtons in vacuum. The engine replaced the Russian KVD-1 that powered the earlier GSLV Mk-I, and it first flew successfully on the GSLV-D5 mission in January 2014. Cryogenic propulsion is more efficient than conventional propellants, and that efficiency is what allows the GSLV to place heavier satellites into the high transfer orbits that navigation and communication satellites need.

Why NVS-04 matters

NVS-04 is the fourth of five second-generation satellites (NVS-01 to NVS-05) being added to NavIC, India's own regional navigation system, which provides positioning, navigation and timing services over India and a region extending about 1,500 km beyond its borders, according to the Press Information Bureau's mission note on GSLV-F18. The NVS satellites carry the L1 signal alongside the existing L5 and S bands. L1 is the band used by GPS, which makes NavIC signals easier to build into ordinary phones and devices.

The constellation rebuild has not been smooth. NVS-01 was launched in May 2023, but NVS-02, launched in January 2025, could not raise its orbit after its oxidiser valves failed to open, and never reached its intended slot. NVS-03, launched on October 30 aboard GSLV-F18, was placed into its intended transfer orbit and completed its first orbit-raising manoeuvre the following day.

What happens next

With the engine cleared, the cryogenic stage for GSLV-F19 can be assembled around it. ISRO did not announce a launch date for the mission in its test update. After NVS-04, one satellite — NVS-05 — remains to complete the five-satellite second-generation series, which ISRO says is intended to boost the coverage, reliability and availability of NavIC services.
nri_angle: A completed NavIC constellation strengthens the navigation services used across transport, maritime and disaster response in India, reducing dependence on foreign systems such as GPS.
